clue.text: Importunes sadly for a new beginning

indicators.note: something done sadly is done badly or wretchedly, so the letters end up disordered

blocks.note: all ten letters are used as fodder

explanation.surface: Someone pesters others mournfully in the hope of making a fresh start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Importunes' reads as the verb of the sentence, but it is only a bag of letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Resumption is starting something again after a pause, which amounts to beginning it over afresh.

clue.text: Kids' barbecue staple

definitions.note: singular definition for a plural answer: ribs as a dish

blocks.note: first meaning: teases, as in to josh someone
second meaning: a bony cut of pork or beef that is a standard grilled dish

explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe makes it look like food for children; read it instead as the verb 'kids' (teases) beside a separate meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: To rib someone is to tease them playfully, and spare ribs are a fixture of any grill menu.

clue.text: Furious as god of love is brought up

indicators.note: in a down entry, bringing something up lifts it so it reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: Eros is the Greek god of love

explanation.surface: Someone is enraged that the god of love has been mentioned in conversation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brought up' suggests raising a topic, but in a down clue it turns the letters upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Sore is an informal, chiefly American word for angry or resentful, so it fits furious.

clue.text: Masculine fellow abandoning jet to attack resident of high altitudes

indicators.note: to abandon is to leave behind, so one letter is dropped from the word it belonged to

blocks.note: M is the standard abbreviation for masculine
a fountain sends up a jet of water
F is the abbreviation for fellow; this is the letter taken away
to go at someone is to attack them, run together as one chunk

explanation.surface: A macho man gives up flying to assault some creature living up in the mountains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jet' looks like an aircraft but is a water spout; GO AT (attack) splits differently from the final word.
explanation.definitionFit: This hoofed animal of the Rockies lives on steep crags far above the tree line, high in thin air.

clue.text: Coati dies, tasting a little spruce? Ever so much

indicators.note: tasting only a little means taking a small portion from within, so the letters sit inside the words

blocks.note: the run of letters spans the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A coati, a raccoon-like animal, dies after nibbling a spruce tree.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a superlative: 'spruce' made 'ever so much' so, that is, the most spruce.
explanation.definitionFit: Spruce means neat and smart; the superlative form, most neat of all, is the answer.

clue.text: Regularly poaches many wildcats

indicators.note: doing something regularly means at fixed intervals, so every other letter is taken

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters
lots means a great many

explanation.surface: A poacher habitually takes large numbers of wild cats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' looks like an adverb about poaching habits, but it picks out the even letters of the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: Ocelots are spotted medium-sized felines of the Americas, an example of untamed cat species.

clue.text: Starters of appetising soups in Fontainebleau? I think not

indicators.note: starters are the opening items, so only the opening letter of each word is kept

blocks.note: the initial letters of four consecutive words

explanation.surface: Would you get tempting soup starters in a French château town? Surely not.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starters' suggests the first course of a meal, which fits the soups, but it means initial letters. Fontainebleau is a French town with a famous palace.
explanation.definitionFit: 'As if!' is a scornful exclamation expressing disbelief, the same dismissive reply as saying that is unlikely.

clue.text: At any cost I organised a kind of holiday

indicators.note: organising things means putting them into a new order, so the letters get rearranged

blocks.note: ten letters from four words used as fodder

explanation.surface: Someone insists they arranged a particular sort of trip whatever it took.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At any cost' reads as an idiom meaning regardless of expense, but together with 'I' it is pure fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A staycation is a vacation spent at home or near home rather than travelling abroad.

clue.text: Perspire if consuming trifles

indicators.note: consuming something breaks it down as it is eaten up, so the letters are digested into a new form

blocks.note: ten letters from two words used as fodder

explanation.surface: Someone sweats whenever they eat trifles, the layered custard and sponge desserts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trifles' looks like the British pudding of sponge, custard and cream, but it means things of little importance.
explanation.definitionFit: Fripperies are showy, frivolous ornaments or unimportant things, so they are trivial knick-knacks of little worth.

clue.text: In retreat, massage, good lingerie and fine wines

indicators.note: a retreating army goes back the way it came, so the word runs backwards

blocks.note: a rub is a massage
G is the abbreviation for good
undies is a casual word for underwear

explanation.surface: A luxury spa weekend away offers massages, nice underwear and good wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In retreat' suggests a spa or getaway, but it turns the massage word backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Burgundy is the wine from a celebrated French region, so several bottles of it are classic quality vintages.

clue.text: Everyman's after snack every so often, and wine

indicators.note: something done every so often happens at intervals, so only alternate letters are kept

blocks.note: first, third and fifth letters
the setter refers to himself, so Everyman is I; ''s after' places it at the end

explanation.surface: The setter is looking for something to nibble now and then, and a glass of wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Everyman's after' means 'Everyman is after': the setter's I comes after the other letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Saki is a variant spelling of sake, the Japanese alcoholic drink brewed from fermented rice.

clue.text: So, a reputable resort offering vehicle for fun

indicators.note: to re-sort is to sort over again, putting things into a different order

blocks.note: twelve letters from three words used as fodder

explanation.surface: A respectable seaside holiday town provides a fun way to get around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resort' looks like a holiday town, which suits the surface, but read as re-sort it rearranges the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A boat used for leisure trips rather than work is a craft whose whole purpose is enjoyment on the water.

clue.text: Shivering, cold, threw up: it happens every four years

indicators.note: shivering is shaking and trembling, so the letters are jumbled about

blocks.note: eleven letters from three words used as fodder

explanation.surface: Someone shivering and vomiting with a chill, followed by the remark that it comes round every leap year.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a list of flu symptoms; the definition is a periodic event, not an illness.
explanation.definitionFit: Football's global championship tournament is held once in each four-year cycle, as is its rugby and cricket equivalent.

clue.text: Showing some leg, Isla to rankle regulator

indicators.note: showing some means displaying a part, so a portion of the following text is on view

blocks.note: the run starts with the first word and ends on the first letter of the last

explanation.surface: A woman called Isla annoys an official by showing a bit of leg.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leg' sits inside the indicator phrase in the surface ('showing some leg') but it is the first word of the hidden run.
explanation.definitionFit: A lawmaker writes the rules that govern and control activity, so is one who regulates.

clue.text: Oldest and shattered, little deer (so Spooner tells us)

indicators.note: Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of words, so his version swaps them

blocks.note: burst means broken apart
fawns are young deer
swap the opening B and F sounds of the two words

explanation.surface: Eldest children are heartbroken over some young deer, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: BURST FAWNS with the initial sounds exchanged is FURST BAWNS, which in a non-rhotic British accent sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The oldest children in families are those who came into the world earliest, ahead of their siblings.

clue.text: Title is stirring for him?

indicators.note: stirring mixes things up, so the letters are churned into a new arrangement

blocks.note: seven letters from two words used as fodder

explanation.surface: A snob thrills at the thought of a grand title.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: a person who is stirred by titles is a snob who favours the privileged.
explanation.definitionFit: An elitist believes a select upper group deserves favour, so rank and honours would excite such a person.

clue.text: About time, forces retreating: that's more intelligent

indicators.note: something retreating goes backwards, so everything before it is read in reverse

blocks.note: re means about or concerning
T is the abbreviation for time
to ram something is to force it

explanation.surface: It is high time the armed forces withdrew; that would be the wiser course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forces' looks like a military noun, but it is a verb here. 'Retreating' applies to the whole string built so far, not just the last word.
explanation.definitionFit: Smart means clever, and its comparative form describes someone with greater brainpower or wit.

clue.text: Enlightenment in, we're told, theguardian.com?

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it spoken, so the sound matters, not the spelling

blocks.note: taken as written
this is a website, a site that sounds like a word for vision

explanation.surface: A reader claims to find wisdom on the Guardian newspaper's website.
explanation.walkthrough: The web address is a cheeky nod to the newspaper that publishes the Everyman; it stands for a site.
explanation.definitionFit: Insight is deep understanding of a matter, the clarity of mind that enlightenment also describes.

clue.text: Reiterate call for Communist to leave?

blocks.note: a Trot is short for a Trotskyist
shouting out is telling someone to leave

explanation.surface: Someone repeatedly demands that a Communist be thrown out.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is the shout itself: a heckler yelling at a Trotskyist to get out.
explanation.definitionFit: To trot out an excuse or argument is to repeat a tired, familiar line yet again.

clue.text: Clues go pear-shaped, sugar

indicators.note: going pear-shaped is British slang for going wrong, so the letters fall into disorder

blocks.note: seven letters from two words used as fodder

explanation.surface: A setter laments that their clues have gone wrong, addressing someone as 'sugar'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go' looks like part of the idiom 'go pear-shaped', but its letters are needed in the fodder. 'Sugar' looks like a term of endearment.
explanation.definitionFit: Glucose is the simple sugar that the body uses as its main source of energy.

clue.text: Grand Old Duke with story about York, ultimately divine

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept
about means around, so one piece wraps around the other

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for grand
O is the abbreviation for old
D is the abbreviation for duke
telling a story can mean telling a lie
the last letter of the city name

explanation.surface: A tale about the Grand Old Duke of York, of the nursery rhyme, ends up seeming heavenly.
explanation.walkthrough: The Grand Old Duke of York marched his men up and down a hill in a children's rhyme; here the phrase is split into abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: Something resembling a deity in power or beauty is heavenly, so like a god.

clue.text: Experimental facility with artist drawing dog

blocks.note: a lab is a laboratory
RA stands for Royal Academician, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts
a doodle is an idle drawing

explanation.surface: In a research laboratory, an artist is sketching a hound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawing dog' reads as an artist sketching a pet, but 'drawing' supplies its own chunk and 'dog' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A labradoodle is a crossbreed of a Labrador retriever and a poodle, a popular family pet.

clue.text: Evil Typhon's necropolitan abode, primarily?

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so the first letter of each word is taken

blocks.note: the initial letters of four consecutive words

explanation.surface: A question about where the monstrous Typhon lies buried.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth Zeus buried the monster Typhon beneath the Sicilian volcano, so the whole clue also describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Mount Etna in Sicily is the volcano under which legend says the giant Typhon was trapped, a tomb-like home.

clue.text: Panic in part of aircraft

blocks.note: first meaning: a state of agitated fluster
second meaning: a hinged section on a wing

explanation.surface: Passengers panic inside an aeroplane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like it places the panic on board, but it only links two meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in a flap is to be agitated, and wing flaps are movable surfaces that adjust lift.

clue.text: Second person in French Resistance, note, to become revolutionary

blocks.note: tu is the French for 'you'
R is the symbol for electrical resistance
N is the abbreviation for note

explanation.surface: A wartime French Resistance agent writes a note urging a comrade to join the uprising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French Resistance' looks like the wartime movement, but the words split: French goes with 'second person', and Resistance alone gives one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Revolution here means rotation, so to go round like a wheel is to rotate or spin.

clue.text: In this puzzle, one is – and isn't – this!

definitions.text: In this puzzle, one is – and isn't – this!

blocks.note: surface reading: a riddle about something both true and untrue of a single thing
setter's reading: 'one' is the number 1, which in this grid starts both an across entry and a down entry

explanation.walkthrough: 1-across runs sideways but 1-down does not, so 'one' both is and isn't lying flat in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Across entries run parallel to the ground line, side to side, which is the meaning of the word.

clue.text: Others snooze

blocks.note: first meaning: the remainder
second meaning: a short sleep or relaxation

explanation.walkthrough: Two unrelated words, each a meaning of the same short word.
explanation.definitionFit: 'The rest' means the remaining people or things, and a rest is a period of sleep or relaxation.

clue.text: Settler working with map: it provides illumination along the way

definitions.text: it provides illumination along the way

indicators.note: working something means kneading or shaping it, so the letters are moulded into a new form

blocks.note: first part of the fodder
second part of the fodder

explanation.surface: A pioneer consults a chart, which lights up the route ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a map is guiding the settler; 'way' is literal, a road.
explanation.definitionFit: A light on a post beside a road shines on the pavement for walkers and drivers at night.
